title: Digit in the Counting String
statement:
Write the positive integers one after another with no separators: "123456789101112131415…". This endless string is the counting string.

Given n, return the digit at position n, counting positions from 1. Return it as a number from 0 to 9.

examples.why: The first nine positions are the digits 1 to 9 themselves.
Positions 10 and 11 hold "10", so position 11 is its 0.
"10" fills 10–11, "11" fills 12–13, "12" fills 14–15. Position 15 is the 2 of 12, not the start of a new number.

hints: How many digits do all the one-digit numbers take up? All the two-digit numbers?
There are 9 numbers with 1 digit, 90 with 2, 900 with 3: block d holds 9·10^(d−1) numbers of d digits each. Skip whole blocks until n falls inside one.
Inside the block of d-digit numbers, the (n − 1) / d -th number after the block start contains the digit, and (n − 1) % d says which of its digits.

explain.intuition:
The counting string is made of blocks: 9 one-digit numbers (9 digits), 90 two-digit numbers (180 digits), 900 three-digit numbers (2 700 digits), and so on. Inside a block every number has the same width, so positions inside it are plain arithmetic.

So first skip whole blocks: subtract each block's digit count from n while n is bigger. Then n is a position inside the block of d-digit numbers, which starts at 10^(d−1). Using a 0-based offset n − 1, the number is start + ⌊(n − 1) / d⌋ and the digit inside it is at index (n − 1) mod d. At most 10 blocks are skipped, so this is effectively constant time.
steps: While n > d · count: subtract d · count from n, then d++, count *= 10, start *= 10.
Return its digit at index (n − 1) mod d, reading from the left.
pitfalls: Using n / d instead of (n − 1) / d. Position 15 is the last digit of 12, not the first digit of 13.
Overflowing 32-bit integers: d · count for d = 9 is 8.1·10⁹. Use 64-bit arithmetic in languages that need it.
Building the string up to n. At 2·10⁹ characters it does not fit in memory.

solutions.title: Walk number by number
solutions.idea: Step through 1, 2, 3, … subtracting each number's width until n lands inside one.

solutions.title: Skip whole blocks of equal width
solutions.idea: Subtract the digit counts of the 1-digit, 2-digit, … blocks, then locate the number and the digit with one division.

solutions.title: Block skip without strings
solutions.idea: Same block skip, but pull the digit out with division and modulo instead of converting the number to text.
solutions.py:
class Solution:
    def digitAt(self, n: int) -> int:
        d, count, start = 1, 9, 1
        while n > d * count:
            n -= d * count
            d += 1
            count *= 10
            start *= 10
        num = start + (n - 1) // d
        from_right = d - 1 - (n - 1) % d
        return num // 10 ** from_right % 10

followups: Write the numbers in base 2 instead of base 10. What changes in the block sizes?
Return the sum of the first n digits of the counting string. How do the blocks help again?
